title: The Cash Flow Forecast That's Already Wrong by August
linkedin:
Most owner-led businesses build one cash flow forecast a year, usually at EOFY, then stop opening it.

By late August, two months of actual trading have happened against that forecast, and in the businesses we work with, the numbers have almost always drifted. Not from one dramatic event, but from a handful of small shifts nobody went back and re-modelled.

Here's a pattern we see often. A business forecasts steady thirty-day collections from its biggest customer back in June. By spring, that customer has quietly drifted to forty five days. Nobody flagged it as a problem because no single late payment looked alarming. But that single shift can strip several weeks of expected cash out of the picture, invisibly, because a forecast built once in June has no mechanism for noticing it happened.

This is the real argument for a rolling forecast over an annual one. A cash flow forecast that gets rebuilt weekly against actuals, typically looking thirteen weeks ahead, catches that kind of drift while it is still a few days, not a full-blown squeeze. It turns a vague sense that things feel tighter than expected into a specific answer: which week the pressure lands, how large it is, and what actually closes the gap.

The businesses that avoid getting caught out here aren't doing anything complicated. They've just made forecasting a weekly habit instead of a June task that gets filed away.

Full piece on the ProfitPulse blog.

A note for business owners across Brisbane, Queensland, New South Wales and Victoria who built a cash flow forecast back at EOFY and haven't looked at it since.

It's a common pattern this time of year. A forecast gets built in June using the best information available at the time, historical collection patterns, known costs, expected seasonal trading. It looks sensible on the page. Then two months of real trading happen against it, and the numbers quietly drift, a customer taking longer to pay, a supplier changing terms, stock ordered earlier than planned for spring. None of this shows up as one dramatic event. It shows up as a tighter week here and there until the gap between the forecast and the bank account becomes hard to explain away.

The businesses that avoid this generally aren't doing anything complicated. They've replaced the once-a-year forecast with a rolling view that gets checked weekly against what's actually happening, so drift gets caught while it is still small and manageable rather than after it has become a genuine squeeze.

If the forecast you built back in June no longer matches what's in the account, that's worth a proper look before spring trading picks up further. Read the full piece on the blog.
